THE MUMMY OF THE 1>F.AU. ' Who fears to speak of Ninety-eight Who blushes at the name; When Cowards mock the patriot s httei Who hangs his head for shame? He's all a knave or hall a slave Who slights his country thus ; But a true man, like you, man, Will fill your glass with us.

We drink the memory of the brave, The faithful and the lew þÿ Some lie far otF hevond the wave, Some sleep in Ireland too ; All þÿ all are gone þÿ hut still lives on The fame of those who died i Al' true men, like you, men, Remember them with pride.

Some on the shores of distant lands Their weary hearts have laid, And bv the stranger's heedless hands Their loi.cly graves were made. But, though their day be lar away Beyond th' Atlantic foam, In true men, like you, men, Their spirit's still at home. The dust of some is Irish earth ; Among their own they rest ; And the same land tliat gave them birth Has caught thein to her breast; And we will pray, that from their ciay Full many a race may start Of true men, like you, men, To act as brave a part.

They rose in dark and evil days To right their native land; They kindled here a living blaze, That nothing shall withstand. Alas ! that might can vanquish right þÿ They fell and passed away ; But true men, like you, men, Are plenty here to-day.

Then here's their memory þÿ may it be For us a guiding light, To cheer our stride lor liberty, And teach us to onile ! Through good and ill, he Ireland still, Though sad as theirs your fate; And true men, be you, men, Like those of Ninety-Eight.

A dra goon regiment commenced the revolt in Portugal they ; mutinied in a body in their country quarters at Torres Novas, about 50 miles from Lisbon, exclaiming, " The Queen and the charter, but down with the ministry '' A council was immediately held at Lisbon, at which it was further discovered that there was a general insurrection throughout the kingdom, and that other regiments were implicated it. in A proclamation was instantly issued for suspending the constitutional guarantees, (corresponding with our habeas corpus,) and for declaring the w hole kingdom to be under martial law. Important Discovery in Egypt þÿ We copy, with a gratification in which we are sure many of our readers will participate, the following interesting statement from the Lite tary Gazette þÿ We rejoice to announce the most important discovery which has probably ever yet been made in the records and iiteiature ot ancient Egypt. Every reader is acqnainted with the history of the celebrated llosetta Stone, and the liappv surmise of Dr. Young, that the trilingual inscriptions on that monument were three versions of the same subject. Following out this idea, mutilated as all the Egyptian part of the stone is, he found that what remained and cou'd be deciphered was identical with the Greek þÿtext. ! leuce our grand key to the translation of the hieroglyphic characters and hieratic writings among the telies of Egypt, on rocks, on the walls of buildings of every kind, on mummy cases, and on papyii; and it is evident th it whatever could add to this key must be of the utmost value. It was interpreted that the Rosctta inscription had also been set up

in other temples ; a mi the learned expressed a hope that in the course of time one or more ol them might reward the tesenreh of zealous antiquaries That hope has been fulfilled- Doctor Lepsius (who had been sent by the King of Prussia to explore the remains of ancient Cgvpt) has discovered another Copy of the liosetta inscription at Meroe. The hieroglyphic portion is unusually perfect, and so, we are informed, is the other Egyptian writing. 'I he three legends may now be compared throughout ; and we hesitate not to sav, that this is likely to create a great revolution, by a vast accession to our means of know ledge, in the literature and history of the country so truly called the cradle of mankind. It is a gratifying circumstance that the noble expedition of the King of Prussia should have met with this return. Copies of the inscription have, we understand, been made tor Berlin ; but the main fact was communicated by letter to his Excellency the Chevalier Bunsen, the Prussian Minister in London. We believe that Dr. Lepsius is directed completely to explore all this upper division of the country, and will not revisit Cairo (ill that is accomplished, probably about April. Alter some repose, the expedition will proceed to S\ i, a, to examine the Egyptian inscriptions there t and from what has already lianspired, there can be no doubt but that a new light wil be thrown over the old world by this royally liberal, auspicious and fortunate eflbrt.

The thing rather takes us by surprise, and we know not w bother to credit it or not. Certainly the belief in the treaty was very strong and general in Texas. We hope it is true. Disinfection. þÿ We are strongly led to believe that nil infectious matter of eveiv description is dependent upon some peculiar combination in which hydrogen gas forms the most essential part, it is now well established that the noxious vapour, the marsh miasma, which has been so destructive to human life, arid the subject of so inanv con. jeotures and speculations, is nothing more nor less than a mixture of carburetted hydro gen In the atmosphere, which is generated rapidly in all putrefactive decompositions, of both vegetable and animal matter. It is in Consequence of the strong affinity of chlorine tor hydrogen that it is capable of decomposing all diseased animal matter Whether it is in the form of a liquid vapour, or of those effluvia that escape the tests of the chemist I hctcfore, tiie carburets of hydrogen which arise from decomposing vegetable matter, is not the vehicle for these miasmata or effiuvial poisons, as has been argued, but is poisonous and deleterious of itself. Hence chlorine has been Used with success to counteract the effect of this gas. and to prevent the communication of conta gious, and the extension ol epidemic disease ; and likewise to render air fit for breathing which was disagreeable or impure. Buildings and ships which contain the natural seeds of disease in consequence ot the presence of this unwholesome air, may readily be disinfected ; it is only necessary to close them tightly, and generate chlorine within, until its smell is sensible in every

part. The chlorine may be either generated directly from manganese or muriatic acid, or procured from chloride of lime In the latter case it is only necessary to steep the chloride of lime in water ; and to rrake the evolution of gas slow, a weak acid may be added. For domestic use, vinegar will answer. It would seem hardly possible tor disease to be propagated even bv actual contact, in an atmosphere that contained a sensible proportion of chlorine gas. Cholera appears to be the only epidemic disease which cannot be influenced by clilo rine. Mr. Editor ! 1 hope there will be nothing found in Ihis letter which could prevent it from pas sing through you before the e\e of the I'ublic, it is written with a good feeling and with sentiments of the greatest respect for those who may hold the contrary opinion. \our readers 1 suppose are aware that a great number of poor persons amongst the free population are allowed by the Burgher Council a certain monthly sum of Money, varying according to each person's want. It has been in contemplation latter! v to withdraw the money from some and to give in its place an allowance of Soup every dav, or every other day, as circumstances will determine. At first sight this plan might appear not only practicable but economical, but when considered in all its hearings, and in relation to those for whose good it is intended, it will he found both useless and extravagant, and therefore Sir 1 am opposed to it on the following ground; I' irst of all if we take into consideration that a lutchen of no ordinary dimensions must be built and furnished with boilers and other culinary requisite?, and if to that he added wages for servants with all their pcriphernnalia ot Pots, Can?, Kettle?, fee., it will be found that the savings, if any, will be very little at the end of the year. But this is a trifling matter in itself, let us pass to other reasons more worthy of attention; some lovers of economy may sav tint tins Soup system has succeeded well in different parts ot Europe, and why not here?

1 he answer is very simple, there is no reason ot parity between the poor here, and the poor at home. In Europe it is absolutely necessary that there should be establishments of this kind, because begging is a trade with many, and were it not that the poor have those public asylums ofrelief, they must either die of hunger or beg from door to door with very little chance of being relieved. But the ease is altogether diflerent here, we have no beggars properly speaking in the West Indies, but we have a class of poor, with whom it is very difficult to deal, lor we have not oniv to consult lor their poverty, but for their feelings also. 1 he great body of the people now on the poor list, are persons to whom Soup would be perfectly useless, there are many poor families here who do not wish to make their poverty known to every one around them, but let them be thrown on the mercy ol the Soup establishment and what more effectual means of exposing them, than to leave them no al ternattve, but either to pine awav in want, or to allow messengers to he seen running backward and forward to them with Soup. It we cannot relieve poverty but by exposing it, it would be better not to relieve it at all, because then it is cruelty and not charity. Besides that, how will Soup pay house rent for the poor ; I am sore our owners of houses would look very bine, if they were to be offered a bowi of Soup, bv wav of House rent How will it clothe respectable females whose only pleasure is not thev Hit the fiat, but

the decent apparel, which enables them to appear abroad and make one amongst the society of their friends ; what will Soup he to persons of this kind, it may he devoured with greediness, it may be sold to liny rum, or it may be thrown to the hogs, but it certainly

S'4\ A T2S, will not alleviate tlie miseries of the poor. People may talk of Soup, but I say that the poor would prefer a live stiver to the best pot ol Soup that could he given theiii, give them that live stiver, and with two or three out of the five, the s w ill with a little herbs manufacture a Soup far superior, and in more accordance with their own taste, than any Soup that can be given them. But ever supposing that bv substituting Soup instead ol money the change Would benefit a few, I say it is not the particular but the general welfare of the community that ought to be taken into consideration. What then would be my advice? simply this, reduce the monthly pension as much as necessity demands, but let the allowance ever so small be given in money, Soup will never do as a substitute for it, il will not telieve distress, it will cause a dissatisfied leeling amongst the people, and in the end it will have to he abandoned as a bad job.' 1 am, Mr. Edilot, Yours fee. The commissioners to Mexico have returned. The precise conditions (or the continuance of the armistice have not transpired, and will perhaps not he made public except from Washington. It is understood that the two countries are to maintain their present pacific positions toward each other until commissioners, to meet at the city of Mexico, have been appointed, and shall have terminated their labors, (or the establishment of a permanent peace between the two nations. The Mexican Government, it is said, is very much disturbed at the prospect of the annexation of Texas to the United States, and well informed persons in Mexico believe that every effort will be made by that Government to make it a condition, on the acknowledgment of the independence of Texas, that she shall remain separate from and independent of the United States. It is thought that no great difficulty would be found in procuring a recognition on this condition, though Santa Ana might be disposed to cavil about me boundary hue between the two countries.

Later from Mexico. Serious difficulties aie anticipated with the French Government by the Mexicans. been reversed ; and now, by the action of her constituted authorities, sustained as it is by popular sentiment, she re-alfirms her desite lor annexation. Tex is herself wills it, and the Executive of the United Stales, concurring with tier, has seen no sufficient reason to avoid the consummation of an act esteemed to he so desirable try both. It cannot be denied that 'Texas is greatly depressed in her energies hv her long- protracted war with Mexico. Under these circumstances, it is hut natural that she should seek for safety and repose under the protection of some stronger power ; and it is equally so that her people should turn to the United States, the land of their birth, in the first instance, in pursuit of such protection. adopt such expedients; or she would hold out the pr tier of discriminating duties in trade 1 and commerce, in order to secure the ueces sary assistance.

Tiie New Dance " The Polka." þÿ Our readers are no doubt aware that this dance has created almost as much sensation in Europe as the dancing epidemv in the middle ages. At Berlin it was, two seasons ago, a perfect mania under the name of Redown, and last season it suddenly dropped ill the very midst of the gay idlers who were collected from evciy part oi Europe at Baden Baden. Thence it travelled to Paris, where it suddenly made its appearance with extraordinary ecl<tl at a reunion at the Conntesse de Pantaloa, and became the ruling mania throughout all classes of society þÿ so that, dancers asked their fair partners to polk ( pniquer .) just as formerly they asked them to waltz.
